newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese refiners cut prices due high inventories.
newsitem.headline: Chinese refiners cut prices due high inventories.

text.p: China has temporarily allowed refiners in its northeastern region to lower ex-refinery prices to help reduce high domestic stockpiles partly caused by smuggling, Chinese traders said on Wednesday.
China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec), China' state refiner and wholesaler of oil products, has lowered ex-refinery prices in the northeast to try to boost sales, traders told Reuters.
Dalian refinery in Liaoning province said it had cut its diesel price by 100 yuan to 2,090 yuan ($251) per tonne.
"We have high inventories," said an official at the Dalian refinery, adding that smuggling into south China had made much cheaper diesel available in that market.
He added that diesel production might have to be reduced.
Officials at the Fushun refinery, also in Liaoning province, said they had been given permission to cut their price but had not yet done so.
The officials added, however, that they might trim prices if more smuggled diesel entered the domestic market.
They also said they had already reduced diesel production and increased gasoline output, though they gave no details.
Traders said smuggled diesel could save about 500 yuan per tonne in duties and other taxes.
Beijing had raised the official ex-refinery price of diesel twice in the fourth quarter of 1996 to 2,190 yuan ($751) per tonne to try to stimulate domestic output.

Falling international prices, heavy imports late last year and early this year and rising domestic stockpiles have caused China's retail diesel prices to drop sharply in the first half of 1997, traders said.
Smuggling activities in the southern provinces of Guangdong and Fujian have aggravated difficulties for domestic refiners, said an official of the State Planning Commission.
Officials said, however, that some areas of the country were not yet affected by high inventories.
An official at the Yanshan refinery in Beijing said local demand for diesel was strong and there was no need to cut diesel prices now.
China was considering limiting diesel fuel imports outside quotas and holding meetings to work out measures to reduce smuggling, officials have said.
"We have reported the smuggling situation to the State Council," an official of Sinopec said by telephone. He did not give further details.
